screens.title: Integer Overflows, Underflows, and SafeMath
screens.subtitle: Why fixed-size integers can break contracts and how to prevent silent wrapping

narration.text: In this lesson we study how fixed-size integers in Solidity can silently wrap and why that is dangerous for smart contracts. You will learn what an overflow and an underflow are, see concrete vulnerable code from older Solidity versions, and then compare two defensive approaches: the community library SafeMath and Solidity's built-in checks starting in version 0.8.0. We'll walk through real examples that show how a counter or token balance can be manipulated when arithmetic wraps around, and then demonstrate how SafeMath reverts the transaction to prevent the wrong state. Finally, we will discuss the unchecked block introduced with Solidity 0.8.0, why a developer might use it for gas savings, and the caution required when opting out of safety. By the end, you'll be able to decide when to use SafeMath, when to rely on compiler checks, and what migration steps matter when updating contract code. Consider the example of incrementing a small uint type to reach its limit: this simple action is the root of many real financial exploits. How will you guard against it in your contracts?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Fixed-size integers can wrap when arithmetic exceeds their range; SafeMath or Solidity 0.8.0+ checks prevent silent vulnerabilities.

screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will explain how fixed-size integer types work in Solidity and why their limited ranges matter. You will identify where integer overflow and underflow bugs appear in contracts — especially in counters, transfers, and supply arithmetic — and why silent wrapping was a common security hazard. You will also know how OpenZeppelin's SafeMath library intercepts dangerous arithmetic in older compiler versions and how to apply its functions in your code. Finally, you will recognize the significance of Solidity 0.8.0's built-in checks and the limited, careful cases where the unchecked block might be used for gas optimization. These skills let you review existing code for subtle arithmetic issues, choose the right protection pattern when writing or migrating contracts, and defend token and accounting logic against attacker-triggered wrapping. Each objective includes a short competency milestone to confirm you can perform the task safely in a real deployment.

screens.title: Fixed-size integers in Solidity
screens.subtitle: What range limits mean and how they define safe arithmetic

narration.text: Solidity exposes fixed-size integer types, meaning each integer occupies a set number of bits and therefore has explicit minimum and maximum values. For example, a uint8 ranges from 0 to 255 and a uint256 ranges from 0 to 2^256 - 1. That limitation matters because any arithmetic that produces a result outside the allowed range cannot be represented correctly. In older compilers that allowed silent wrapping, that arithmetic simply wrapped: adding one to the maximum yielded the minimum, and subtracting one from zero yielded the maximum. In practice this means simple operations like incrementing a counter or reducing a balance require careful consideration before trusting them. A key misconception is to assume integer types are unbounded; they are not. When you select a type like uint8 for storage or gas savings, you accept the smaller range and the higher risk of wrapping. Use the largest reasonable type, or validate inputs and use checked arithmetic, especially for balances, token supply, vote weights, and any critical accounting variable. A quick concrete example: if a token's total supply is equal to type(uint256). max and you call a mint function that adds a positive amount, the sum would overflow and wrap in older versions, corrupting supply math. Always pair type choice with defensive checks or use compilers that enforce arithmetic safety. How will you reason about the integer ranges in your next contract design?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Fixed-size integers have explicit ranges; choosing a type creates upper and lower bounds that define safe arithmetic.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Fixed-size integers
Fixed-size integers in Solidity
How bit width defines numeric range and risk.
Range examples: uint8 = 0–255; uint256 = 0–2^256-1
What this means
  • Each type has a fixed numeric range determined by bit width.
  • Arithmetic outside that range cannot be represented correctly.
  • Selecting smaller types trades storage/gas for a narrower safe range.
  • Critical accounting variables should use types with safe margins or checks.
Analogy
Think of each integer type as a cup with fixed volume; pouring beyond it spills in an unexpected way unless you check the amount.
Concrete example
If a uint8 counter is 255 and you perform an increment, older compilers wrap the value to 0. In a token system, that same wrap could lead to an attacker creating a balance anomaly or bypassing a check.
// uint8 example
uint8 counter = 255;
counter++; // wraps to 0 in older compilers
Key Takeaway

Fixed-size types limit safe values; when designing contract storage or arithmetic, assume ranges are enforced by you or the compiler.

screens.title: Overflow vs Underflow
screens.subtitle: Contrast the two wrapping behaviors and common misconceptions

narration.text: Overflow and underflow are two sides of the same wrapping behavior caused by hitting a type's numeric limits. An overflow happens when a computation results in a value above the maximum representable number, and underflow happens when a computation goes below the minimum. For unsigned types that minimum is zero, so subtracting more than the current value causes the number to wrap to the type's maximum. A common misconception is that these events always throw or produce an explicit error; in Solidity versions before 0.8.0, they did not — the arithmetic wrapped silently and execution continued. That silent behavior is what made overflows and underflows so dangerous in financial contracts. Consider a balance subtraction where a malicious input causes underflow: the balance may wrap to a very large number, and subsequent logic might treat that as a legitimate balance. The practical difference between overflow and underflow is what side of the range you cross, but their security impact is the same: corrupted state and exploitable logic. Always check inputs, prefer safer arithmetic, and when reading old contracts, treat any unchecked arithmetic as a red flag. What boundary checks will you add to your code to avoid these traps?

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: Overflow increases past max; underflow decreases below min. Both corrupt state when unchecked and were silent before Solidity 0.8.0.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Overflow vs Underflow
Overflow vs Underflow
Understand the difference and why silent wrapping is hazardous.
Overflow
Occurs when result > max value. Example: uint8 255 + 1 wraps to 0 in older compilers.
Underflow
Occurs when result < min value. Example: uint8 0 - 1 wraps to 255.
Misconception
Assuming arithmetic always reverts — only true from 0.8.0 onward.
Security impact
Wrapped values can become attacker-controlled and break invariants.
Practical check
Validate ranges and use checked arithmetic for balances and totals.
Key Takeaway

Overflow and underflow are boundary-crossing errors that previously wrapped silently; treat unchecked arithmetic as a high-severity risk in financial logic.

screens.title: VulnerableCounter (Solidity ^0.7.0)
screens.subtitle: Examine a minimal contract that demonstrates silent wrapping

narration.text: Let's step through a compact vulnerable example to make the problem concrete. A simple contract declares a small uint8 counter and exposes increment and decrement functions that use the built-in ++ and -- operators. In a Solidity compiler before 0.8.0 those operations do not include overflow checks. That means if the counter reaches its maximum value and someone calls increment, the value will wrap to zero without a revert. Conversely, decrement from zero wraps to the maximum. This behavior is silent and may be unnoticed by higher-level logic that assumes monotonic growth or safe subtraction. The concrete danger appears when that counter controls funds, permissions, or supply calculations. An attacker can trigger wrap-around by orchestrating calls or by exploiting logic that allows the counter to reach its boundary. Here is the vulnerable code. Read it and try to predict the state after incrementing at 255 or decrementing at 0. Notice as you read which operations lack guards and which storage variables would be corrupted during a wrap. The key exercise is to reproduce the wrap in a 0.7. x environment, then refactor the operations so they call checked arithmetic instead. What invariant would you add to this contract to prove it safe?

keyIdea.title: Vulnerability example
keyIdea.text: Simple increment/decrement on small types can silently wrap in Solidity <0.8.0, corrupting state when those values guard important logic.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › VulnerableCounter
Vulnerable contract (0.7.x)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.7.0; // Vulnerable to silent overflow/underflow

contract VulnerableCounter {
    uint8 public count = 0; // Small type for easy demonstration

    function increment() public {
        count++; // Potential overflow
    }

    function decrement() public {
        count--; // Potential underflow
    }

    function add(uint8 a, uint8 b) public pure returns (uint8) {
        return a + b; // Potential overflow
    }

    function subtract(uint8 a, uint8 b) public pure returns (uint8) {
        return a - b; // Potential underflow
    }
}
Explanation & implications
  • count++ and count-- have no safety checks in 0.7.x; they can wrap silently.
  • Pure arithmetic functions returning a + b or a - b can overflow/underflow without revert.
  • If this counter guards funds or permissions, the wrapped value can open an exploit path.
Common Mistake
Assuming small demo counters are harmless; in production they often connect to critical logic and require checks.
Key Takeaway

Any unchecked arithmetic in pre-0.8.0 Solidity is a potential severity one issue for financial or state-critical code.

screens.title: VulnerableToken: transfer and burn pitfalls
screens.subtitle: How unchecked subtraction can let users withdraw funds they don't have

narration.text: Now consider a minimal token contract that performs subtraction on balances without any require guard. In the VulnerableToken example, transfer and burn directly decrement balances and totalSupply. If an attacker calls transfer with an amount greater than their balance under older compilers, the subtraction wraps to a large value, and the contract proceeds to credit the recipient. The attacker suddenly appears to have a huge balance, or totalSupply becomes corrupted after a burn underflow. This demonstrates the real-world impact: silent wrapping turns a small arithmetic oversight into a loss of funds or a total ledger corruption. The right defense in a 0.7. x environment is to check conditions before arithmetic and to use SafeMath functions which revert on overflow or underflow. When you execute the hands-on activity, you should be able to deploy this vulnerable token in Remix with compiler 0.7. x, demonstrate the wrap by triggering a transfer that underflows, and see how an attacker could then duplicate funds. That concrete exercise makes the danger tangible and helps you prioritize fixes in real codebases. VulnerableToken: transfer and burn pitfalls means unchecked subtraction in token transfers or burns can underflow and enable attackers to create or steal funds in older solidity compilers.. In practical terms, how unchecked subtraction can let users withdraw funds they don't have. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Token risk
keyIdea.text: Unchecked subtraction in token transfers or burns can underflow and enable attackers to create or steal funds in older Solidity compilers.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › VulnerableToken
VulnerableToken: transfer and burn pitfalls
Unchecked subtraction can make a user suddenly hold a huge balance when wrapping occurs.
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.7.0;

contract VulnerableToken {
    string public name = "VulnerableToken";
    string public symbol = "VNT";
    uint256 public totalSupply = 1000;
    mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

    constructor() {
        balances[msg.sender] = totalSupply;
    }

    function transfer(address _to, uint256 _amount) public returns (bool) {
        // No check for _amount > balances[msg.sender]
        balances[msg.sender] -= _amount; // underflow possible
        balances[_to] += _amount;
        return true;
    }

    function burn(uint256 _amount) public {
        balances[msg.sender] -= _amount; // underflow possible
        totalSupply -= _amount; // totalSupply underflow possible
    }
}
Concrete exploit
Call transfer with _amount larger than your balance; balances[msg.sender] underflows to a huge number and the recipient gets credited.
Mitigation
In 0.7.x use require checks or SafeMath's sub to revert on invalid amounts.
Key Takeaway

Token arithmetic must be guarded; underflows can produce attacker-controlled amounts and should be prevented by checks or SafeMath in older compilers.

screens.title: OpenZeppelin's SafeMath
screens.subtitle: How SafeMath prevents wrapping in Solidity <0.8.0

narration.text: SafeMath is a community-standard library that provides wrappers for arithmetic operations which check for overflow and underflow before performing the operation. In practice, functions like add, sub, mul, div, and mod perform a safety check and revert the transaction if the result would overflow or underflow. You apply SafeMath with the 'using SafeMath for' directive so that arithmetic calls read naturally as member functions on the numeric type. For example, instead of writing count = count + 1 you write count = count. add(1); SafeMath reverts rather than allowing a wrapped result. This library was central to secure contract development for projects compiled with Solidity prior to 0.8.0. A common misconception is that SafeMath changes the underlying types; it does not — it only wraps operations with checks. When migrating older codebases, replacing raw arithmetic with SafeMath calls is a practical first step that preserves intended behavior and immediately prevents many classes of exploit. The library also documents that it is intended as a defensive guard for balances, totals, and similar critical arithmetic. OpenZeppelin's SafeMath means safemath adds explicit overflow/underflow checks to arithmetic operations, reverting before invalid results are stored.. In practical terms, how safemath prevents wrapping in solidity <0.8.0. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SafeMath purpose
keyIdea.text: SafeMath adds explicit overflow/underflow checks to arithmetic operations, reverting before invalid results are stored.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › SafeMath
OpenZeppelin's SafeMath
A defensive wrapper that reverts on arithmetic errors for older compilers.
Why it helps
  • Reverts the transaction before storing an invalid result.
  • Provides add, sub, mul, div, and mod helpers with checks.
  • Integrates via 'using SafeMath for' for readable calls.
How to use
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.7.0;

import "@openzeppelin/contracts/utils/math/SafeMath.sol";

contract SafeCounter {
    using SafeMath for uint256;
    uint256 public totalValue = 0;

    function addToTotal(uint256 _amount) public {
        totalValue = totalValue.add(_amount);
    }
}
Pro tip
When updating legacy code, adding SafeMath calls is a quick and safe improvement that avoids a full language upgrade immediately.
Key Takeaway

SafeMath provides explicit guards that convert silent wrapping into safe reverts in Solidity versions prior to 0.8.0.

screens.title: SafeCounter using SafeMath (0.7.x)
screens.subtitle: A direct refactor that prevents overflow and underflow

narration.text: Here we refactor the earlier VulnerableCounter into a SafeCounter that uses OpenZeppelin's SafeMath. The key change is replacing raw arithmetic and ++/-- operators with SafeMath calls like add and sub. Because SafeMath reverts when an operation would overflow or underflow, the contract's state cannot silently wrap into an invalid value. Note how 'using SafeMath for uint8' and 'using SafeMath for uint256' apply the helper functions directly on variables, keeping code readable while introducing safety. This pattern is especially important for balances, totals, and counters used in access or distribution logic. Another practical point: SafeMath's revert consumes gas, but so does recovering from an exploit; the tradeoff is strongly in favor of safety. When you implement SafeMath in your tests, reproduce the failing case from the vulnerable contract and then show the same call now reverts. This concrete difference demonstrates why SafeMath became a community staple for pre-0.8.0 code. As a closing thought, consider whether you would keep SafeMath after migrating the project to a newer compiler or remove it to simplify code while preserving tests to ensure consistent behavior. SafeCounter using SafeMath (0.7.x) means replace raw arithmetic with safemath's add/sub to convert silent wrapping into explicit reverts on error.. In practical terms, a direct refactor that prevents overflow and underflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor pattern
keyIdea.text: Replace raw arithmetic with SafeMath's add/sub to convert silent wrapping into explicit reverts on error.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › SafeCounter
SafeCounter example
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.7.0;

import "@openzeppelin/contracts/utils/math/SafeMath.sol";

contract SafeCounter {
    using SafeMath for uint256; // Apply SafeMath to uint256
    using SafeMath for uint8;   // Apply SafeMath to uint8

    uint8 public count = 0;
    uint256 public totalValue = 0;

    function increment() public {
        count = count.add(1);
    }

    function decrement() public {
        count = count.sub(1);
    }

    function addToTotal(uint256 _amount) public {
        totalValue = totalValue.add(_amount);
    }
}
Notes and proof
  • SafeMath functions revert before a value would wrap, preserving contract invariants.
  • Using SafeMath for small types like uint8 still matters because the range is tiny.
  • Testing should include boundary cases: max value + 1 and 0 - 1.
Testing step
Deploy with 0.7.x, call increment at max and confirm the transaction reverts rather than wrapping.
Key Takeaway

SafeMath is straightforward to integrate and is a practical defense for legacy compilers.

screens.title: Solidity 0.8.0+: Built-in overflow/underflow checks
screens.subtitle: How compiler-level safety changes the development story

narration.text: Solidity 0.8.0 changed the default behavior for arithmetic by inserting automatic overflow and underflow checks into compiled operations. From that version onward, a + b or x++ will cause the transaction to revert if the result cannot be represented in the declared type. This change simplifies development because most explicit SafeMath calls are no longer required to secure basic arithmetic. However, the language designers also provided unchecked blocks so developers can opt out of checks for specific operations when they intentionally want wrapping behavior or need micro-optimizations. The practical implication is that migration from an older compiler should include an audit of intentional wraps and of any code that previously relied on silent behavior. Removing SafeMath from a migrated codebase is often safe but should be accompanied by tests and attention to unchecked blocks. A common oversight is to blindly rely on unchecked to cut gas without assuring the operands cannot cross boundaries. Compiler checks shift the burden from explicit library calls to careful decisions about when to disable those checks and why. When migrating, balance simplicity, safety, and the small measured gas gains from unchecked code.

keyIdea.title: Compiler safety
keyIdea.text: From 0.8.0, arithmetic operations revert on overflow/underflow by default; unchecked blocks opt out at the developer's risk.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Solidity 0.8.0+
Solidity 0.8.0+: Built-in checks
Arithmetic now reverts by default on invalid results.
What changed
  • Plain arithmetic operations include overflow/underflow checks.
  • Transactions revert automatically instead of silently wrapping.
  • Developers no longer need SafeMath for basic arithmetic safety.
Unchecked blocks
You can opt out of checks for a block using 'unchecked { ... }'. Use this only when you can prove the operation is safe or intentionally want wrapping, such as specific low-level loops or cryptographic code that depends on wrapping semantics.
Migration note
When moving code to 0.8.x, remove redundant SafeMath calls where they only duplicated compiler checks, but retain tests to prove behavior remains correct.
Key Takeaway

Compiler-level checks improve safety and simplify code, but unchecked blocks reintroduce risk and require careful justification.

screens.title: The unchecked block
screens.subtitle: When and why you might disable compiler checks

narration.text: The unchecked block in Solidity 0.8.0+ is a tool that allows developers to execute arithmetic without automatic overflow or underflow checks. This can reduce gas when you are certain the operation cannot overflow, or when wrapping semantics are desired. However, unchecked reintroduces the exact risks SafeMath addressed: silent wrapping and corrupted state. Use unchecked only when you have provable bounds on inputs and outputs, and ideally when those assumptions are supported by earlier guards or by invariants verified in tests. For instance, a tight loop that increments a counter and is known to stay within limits might justify unchecked for micro-optimization, but that justification should be documented and tested. A common mistake is to wrap many operations with unchecked to save a small amount of gas across the contract; that multiplies the risk surface and makes future changes hazardous. The safer default is to keep checks on and only apply unchecked to narrowly scoped, well-tested operations. When you do use unchecked, include unit tests that assert invariants at boundary values. The unchecked block means unchecked disables safety checks — use it only when you can prove bounds and have tests to validate the assumption.. In practical terms, when and why you might disable compiler checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Unchecked rule
keyIdea.text: unchecked disables safety checks — use it only when you can prove bounds and have tests to validate the assumption.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Unchecked Block
The unchecked block
Opt out of compiler checks for deliberate, constrained use cases.
Example usage
unchecked {
  count++; // no revert on overflow here
}
When to use
Narrowly scoped loops with proven bounds, or algorithms that intentionally rely on wrapping (rare).
When not to use
Never apply unchecked to general accounting, token transfers, or operations that depend on invariants without tests.
Key Takeaway

Unchecked blocks can save gas but reintroduce wrapping risks; use them sparingly and defend them with tests and documentation.

screens.title: Migrating vulnerable code to safe arithmetic
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step checklist for refactoring and testing

narration.text: When migrating a codebase that was written for Solidity 0.7. x or earlier, follow a deliberate process to remove arithmetic risks. First, run static analysis and tests to identify operations that perform unchecked arithmetic — look for +, -, ++, --, and inline arithmetic in transfer or burn logic. Second, for each hotspot, determine whether to use SafeMath (if staying on pre-0.8.0) or rely on compiler checks after upgrading to 0.8. x. Third, add unit tests that exercise boundary values: max + 1 and 0 - 1, and assert that operations revert rather than wrap. Fourth, if you remove SafeMath after migrating, keep the tests and scan for any unchecked blocks you might have added; these become code-review targets. Fifth, document any unchecked usage with a comment explaining why bounds are guaranteed and link to tests proving the claim. Finally, deploy to a testnet and monitor for unexpected edge-case behavior. This process reduces human error and makes migrations auditable. Which step will you prioritize first in your next upgrade? Migrating vulnerable code to safe arithmetic
A step-by-step checklist to refactor and verify arithmetic safety.
Steps

  2. Decide SafeMath (if staying on <0.8.0) or upgrade to 0.8.x to rely on checks.
  3. Add unit tests for boundary cases and assert reverts.
  4. Document any unchecked blocks and justify proofs or tests.
  5. Deploy to testnet and monitor for edge-case reports.
Quick sanity checks
  • Are all transfers guarded?
  • Is totalSupply protected from overflow?
  • Do tests include max and zero boundaries?
Key Takeaway

A small, repeatable migration process reduces risk and makes the change auditable and testable.

screens.title: Best practices and common mistakes
screens.subtitle: A checklist to avoid integer vulnerabilities in your contracts

narration.text: To close the lessons, adopt a short set of best practices that prevents most integer-related vulnerabilities. First, prefer using sufficiently wide integer types for critical accounting variables; avoid tiny types unless you have a specific reason. Second, validate all external inputs before arithmetic, especially amounts provided by users. Third, for projects using pre-0.8.0 compilers, use SafeMath for all arithmetic that affects balances, totals, or permissioned counters. Fourth, when using Solidity 0.8.0+, rely on built-in checks, but document and test any unchecked blocks. Fifth, write boundary tests that explicitly check max + 1 and 0 - 1 behavior and assert reverts. Sixth, avoid optimistic assumptions that values will never hit extremes; attackers can force boundary conditions. Common mistakes include removing SafeMath without adding tests, using unchecked to save gas without justification, and choosing tiny integer types for convenience. Following these practices makes arithmetic errors visible during development instead of catastrophic in production. Which practice will you add to your repo's security checklist today? Best practices and common mistakes means prefer wide types, validate inputs, use safemath on old compilers, rely on 0.8.0 checks with caution, and add boundary tests.. In practical terms, a checklist to avoid integer vulnerabilities in your contracts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Here are the core concepts to keep at hand as you write and review Solidity code.
